topic: Research group / lab website patterns — people pages, alumni-with-placement, news feeds, research thrusts, projects/sponsors, joining pages, and group-scale publications — studied across 25+ real lab sites, to inform the RAFT research-team page and the students/alumni sections of satishregonda.in
key_findings: ALUMNI WITH CURRENT PLACEMENT is the single highest-value, most-often-botched pattern. The four best implementations I verified: (1) Princeton Visual AI Lab — alumni split by degree tier, each entry is degree + years + thesis title in italics + current job, e.g. 'Dr. Sunnie S. Y. Kim, PH.D. DEGREE 2025, _Advancing Responsible AI with Human-Centered Evaluation_, Research Scientist at Apple'. (2) Kording Lab — a literal 3-column table: name | role and tenure | current position, e.g. 'Tony Liu | Graduate Student (2018-2024) | Assistant Professor of Computer Science, Mount Holyoke College'. (3) AIT ETH Zurich — 'Previous Members' grouped by departure year with 'Now at' phrasing: '2020 - 2025 | Dr. Zijian Dong | Now at PicoXR (ByteDance)'. (4) Centre for Hydrology, U. Saskatchewan — a table of name | degree, year | thesis title | current position: 'Warren Helgason | PhD, 2009 | Energy Fluxes at the Air-Snow Interface | Associate Professor, Department of Agricultural and Bioresource Engineering, U of S'.

ALUMNI DONE BADLY, verified, so we know exactly what to avoid: Stanford HCI Group shows alumni as photo + name only with no links and no placement ('Adrian Graham') — maximum visual weight, zero information. UW Interactive Data Lab shows alumni as hyperlinked names only. Terrer Lab's team page renders alumni as an undifferentiated comma-blob ('Leila Mirzagholi Na Chen Yanlei Feng Trevor Cambron...'). WRE Lab (Northeastern) has an 'Alumni' heading with exactly one name and no details, plus an empty 'Postdoc' tier header with nobody under it. The lesson: a photo on an alumnus costs a lot and says nothing; a placement line costs nothing and says everything.

TIERED INFORMATION DENSITY is how labs keep a people page readable as headcount grows. Bhamla Lab (Georgia Tech) is the cleanest example: Research Scientists & Postdocs and Grad Students get full cards (headshot, one-line research description, email, Google Scholar link, expandable 'Read more →'); Staff gets text only; 46 undergraduates get name + major abbreviation only ('ChBE', 'BME'); 4 high-school interns get a bare list. Same page, four densities. UW IDL does a two-density version: a headshot grid of current members at the top, a detail list below, alumni text-only.

MISSING PHOTOS: CMU HCII's PhD directory serves a generic grey silhouette placeholder (`default_images/silhouette2.png`) for members without a headshot — it visually reads as 'this person doesn't matter' and makes the page look half-built. Every site I found that handles it well simply drops the photo for that tier rather than substituting a placeholder (UW IDL alumni, Bhamla undergrads, Saskatchewan alumni table, ORI's entirely photo-free directory).

PHOTO SHAPE has no industry consensus, which means the design is free to choose — the discriminator is CONSISTENCY of crop and treatment, not shape. AIT ETH uses circular avatars left-aligned in a single-column list. CMU HCII uses 600x400 landscape crops. Princeton Visual AI pairs a photo with a linked name in a grid. Since a hydrology group's photos will arrive as phone snapshots of wildly varying quality, a fixed aspect ratio plus a unifying treatment (desaturation, a duotone tint, or a consistent warm-grey background) is what will save the page.

GROUP PHOTO WITH ROW-BY-ROW NAME CAPTIONS: ETH Zurich's Land-Climate Dynamics group (Sonia Seneviratne) shows two dated group photographs — August 2024 and 2023 — with names listed by row position in the caption. It's near-zero maintenance, keeps every face on the page, and is dramatically more alive than 12 isolated headshots. Keeping the previous year's photo alongside the current one is itself a signal of continuity.

NEWS FEED FORMAT, densest verified example: AIT ETH Zurich uses DD.MM.YY dating ('04.05.26'), one small thumbnail per item (usually the person's headshot or a conference logo), 1–2 lines of text, and an unbroken reverse-chronological run from 2026 back to 2013 with NO year headers. Sample items verbatim: 'Seyedmorteza Sadat passed the doctoral exam. Congratulations!', 'We have 4 papers accepted at ICCV 2025.', 'Three new papers accepted at ACM SIGCHI 2015.'

HOW LABS KEEP A SPARSE NEWS FEED FROM LOOKING DEAD — the answer is item-type mix, not posting frequency. Terrer Lab's news mixes departures ('Farewell to Sara, Diego and Shuai'), fellowships ('Ruofei Jia has been awarded a Martin Fellowship for the 2026–2027 academic year'), meta-news ('We have just launched a new Terrer Lab website'), and recognitions ('César Terrer has been named to Clarivate's 2025 Highly Cited Researchers list'). Eight event types (paper accepted, student joined, student defended, award, talk/conference, fieldwork, grant, media hit) generate 15–25 items a year from a group of twelve without anyone 'writing content'.

HOMEPAGE-AS-TIMELINE: Princeton Visual AI Lab's homepage is dominated by a section literally headed 'RECENT TIMELINE', reverse-chronological from July 2026 back to August 2025. Each entry carries a date, a linked achievement or paper title, venue + year, author names, and a small image. There is no separate 'news' page competing with it — the feed IS the homepage. Highest signal-to-effort structure I saw for a group page, and it's what makes the site feel current on first paint.

RESEARCH THRUSTS WITHOUT STOCK ICONS — three verified approaches. (a) Method-based prose thrusts, Terrer Lab: 'Field measurements — Repeated soil and biomass sampling at sites across the world's biomes'; 'Satellites & remote sensing — Global observations of vegetation, carbon, and land-cover change from space'; 'Machine learning & synthesis — Meta-analysis and statistical models that scale field data to the globe'. (b) Custom-drawn SVG marks, Ink & Switch: four pillars (Local-first Software, Malleable Software, Programmable Ink, Universal Version Control), each with a bespoke hand-drawn glyph, not a stock icon set. (c) Pure text, Princeton Visual AI: three thrusts as plain headed text lines with zero graphics, letting the publication list below carry the visual load.

HERO AS A QUESTION, not a mission statement. Terrer Lab (MIT, climate/carbon — the closest domain analogue I found) opens with 'How much carbon can land hold, and for how long?' followed by the method sentence 'We combine field measurements, satellites, and machine learning to quantify the terrestrial carbon sink — and how climate change is reshaping it.' Compare UW IDL's more conventional 'our mission is to enhance people's ability to understand and communicate data...'. The question form is editorially stronger and instantly non-templated.

PROGRESSIVE VISUAL RICHNESS (Google DeepMind research page): flagship 'Breakthroughs' get full-width 1440x810 hero imagery; 'Latest News' gets 704x704 thumbnails in a grid with category tags ('Science', 'Research') and month-year dates ('September 2026'); publications get plain text links with no imagery at all. Visual weight is allocated by importance. The template-trap is giving every item an identical card.

PUBLICATIONS AT GROUP SCALE, best verified pattern (UW Interactive Data Lab): grouped by year, reverse-chron; each entry is thumbnail + linked title + author names each individually hyperlinked + venue and year + a row of resource chips (PDF, Software, Demo, Video, Website) + an award badge where earned ('Best Paper Award', 'Honorable Mention'). Stanford HCI Group adds action chips like 'TRY IT!' and '[PROJECT]'. The resource-chip row is precisely what makes a publication list read as a working lab rather than a CV paste.

FUNDED PROJECTS AND SPONSOR CREDIT — two distinct verified models. (1) SCI-Hy group (Utah State) splits projects into 'Active' and 'Completed' as image cards and folds the funder into the project title itself: 'CIROH: Advance water management-hydrologic model coupling to improve hydrologic forecasting in managed watersheds'. No grant numbers, no logos, no PI-role field. (2) Princeton Visual AI puts a single 'ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS' block at the foot of the homepage listing sponsors tagged '(current/ongoing)' vs '(past)'. Nobody I fetched displays grant numbers prominently — they are CV material, not website material.

JOINING PAGE, gold standard (Terrer Lab): rather than 'we are always looking for motivated students', it names four SPECIFIC external fellowships with deadlines and a fit note — NOAA Climate & Global Change Postdoctoral Fellowship (closes October 16, 2026, 'A strong fit for the lab'); MIT Postdoctoral Fellowship Program for Engineering Excellence (deadline ~late January); Marie Skłodowska-Curie Global Fellowships (~mid-September, 'the natural route for a European researcher to work with us'); Schmidt Science Fellows (~spring, for those 'pivoting into a new field') — and tells candidates to make contact early so they can 'shape the proposal and research plan together'.

JOINING PAGE, most concrete terms (WRE Lab, Northeastern): states funding through RA/TA support for up to five years, competitive stipend, tuition waiver, health insurance, conference funding; names TWO application routes with two different deadlines (Marine & Environmental Science, December 1; Civil & Environmental Engineering, December 15); notes 'While an M.S. is preferred, it is not required'; and adds 'Candidates from historically and currently marginalized groups are particularly encouraged to apply.'

PERSONALITY TOKENS in people metadata — UW IDL appends one or two non-research interests to each person's line: 'Leilani Battle, Professor, UW CSE, Databases, Visualization, HCI, Zombies, Disc Golf' and 'Josh Horowitz, PhD Student, UW CSE, Dynamic Media, End-User Programming, Bikes, Maps'. Two words per person, enormous aliveness payoff, and impossible for a generic template to fake.

A DEDICATED 'LAB LIFE' PAGE is the cheapest aliveness lever verified. Terrer Lab's is one line of framing — 'Field trips, dinners, graduations, and the day-to-day of a small international group' — plus captioned candids ('Pizza & Science in our new group space') and a closing CTA, 'Want to be part of it? See Join us.' It costs nothing to maintain and it is the section a prospective student actually reads.

PAST MEMBERS INLINE vs SEPARATE: MIT Media Lab's City Science group keeps past members in the SAME alphabetical roster, tagged in place — 'Chance Jiajie Li, Research Affiliate, Past Member'. It avoids a graveyard page but makes the current roster harder to scan. For a ~12-person group, a same-page anchor section beats both a separate alumni page (which nobody visits) and inline tagging (which muddies the roster).

DIRECTORY TREATMENT DOES NOT SCALE DOWN: Oxford Robotics Institute's people page uses an A–Z letter index plus role filters (All staff / Academic staff / Research staff / DPhil Candidates / Admin & Support Staff), no photos, entries like 'Maurice Fallon — Professor of Robotics; PI of Dynamic Robot Systems Group'. This works for 100+ people and reads cold and institutional at 12. RAFT should NOT be built as a filterable directory.

THE RAW MATERIAL FOR A PRINCETON-GRADE ALUMNI TABLE ALREADY EXISTS on the current Google Site. Its Students page already lists 9 current PhD scholars with research topics ('Saipriya SR, Understanding urban hydroclimatology and modelling of urban floods for the city Hyderabad, India'), 6 graduated PhDs with full thesis titles and viva dates ('Vimal Chandra Sharma, Streamflow Forecasting and Flood Inundation Modelling Framework in the Lower Godavari River Basin, India, viva-voice was done in September 2021'), 9 graduated MTech students with project titles and years, and 3 UG mini-projects. The ONLY missing field is current placement — collect that one column and the alumni section immediately outclasses Stanford HCI's.

RAFT's own content is already well-defined and specific: RAFT = 'Rainfall-runoff Analysis modelling and Forecasting Tools (RAFT) Research Team'; goal is 'a flood information system for both cities and riverine areas' enabling dialogue between scientists, engineers, policymakers and citizens; current roster is 6 PhD scholars (Surya Kiran, Padmini, Saipriya, Lagnajeet, Mohan, Vamshi) and 3 MTech students (Swagatam, Kanishka, Shruti); and it has a genuinely distinctive citizen-science asset — the SnapFlood mobile application plus a Google Form and social channels for uploading 'flood relevant media'. SnapFlood deserves to be a named product block, not a bullet.

raftwaters.in DOES NOT CURRENTLY RESOLVE — a DNS lookup failed (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND) on 2026-09-04. Any 'visit the RAFT site' link will be dead on launch day unless that domain is stood up first. Design the RAFT page to be complete and self-sufficient without the outbound link.
recommendations: Build RAFT as ONE long scrolling page with a sticky in-page anchor rail (What RAFT is / Themes / SnapFlood & tools / People / Alumni / Projects & funding / Publications / Join), not as a sub-site. At 12 people a directory-style multi-page structure (Oxford Robotics style) reads institutional and cold; a single rich page reads like a team.

Open the RAFT page with a QUESTION plus a method sentence, Terrer-Lab style, in place of a mission statement. Something in the register of 'How much water will Indian cities and rivers see, and how soon can we tell anyone?' followed by 'We collect, model and forecast rainfall and runoff for Indian cities and river basins — and turn it into information people can act on.' The existing Google Site text ('collection, analysis, modelling, and development and dissemination of products') is the raw material; it needs an editor, not a rewrite.

Give RAFT 4 research thrusts as prose blocks with real field/model/satellite imagery, NOT stock icons. Suggested from the existing content: (1) Streamflow forecasting for Indian river basins; (2) Urban flooding — Hyderabad, Kochi; (3) Hydroclimatology and monsoon extremes; (4) Data, ML and citizen observations. Two sentences each, plus a 'related people / papers / projects' link row. If a mark is wanted per thrust, commission four hand-drawn SVG glyphs (Ink & Switch model) rather than buying an icon set.

Make SnapFlood a named product block with its own visual — a phone screenshot, an app-store/Play link, and a one-line 'what it does'. It is the most distinctive thing RAFT has and the current site buries it in a paragraph. DeepMind's progressive-richness rule applies: this gets the big image; papers get plain text.

PEOPLE: three densities on one page. (a) PI: a short block, one photo, and a link back to Satish's own bio — the RAFT page must never repeat his CV. (b) PhD scholars: card with photo, name, cohort/start year, one-line research topic taken verbatim from the existing Students page, email, and Scholar/ORCID links where they exist. (c) MTech and UG/interns: name + year + project title in a compact text list, no photos. This is the Bhamla Lab structure and it is what will keep the page readable when the group is 25 people.

PHOTOS: enforce a single aspect ratio (1:1 square or a 4:5 portrait) plus one unifying treatment — a light desaturation and a consistent warm-grey background — so that phone snapshots and formal ID photos sit together without looking chaotic. NEVER ship a grey silhouette placeholder (CMU HCII's mistake). If a person has no photo, render a typographic tile: their initials in the site's display face on a tinted block. It will read as intentional rather than missing.

ADD A GROUP PHOTO with row-by-row name captions, ETH Land-Climate-Dynamics style, and date it ('RAFT, IIT Hyderabad, October 2026'). Keep last year's alongside it. This is the highest-aliveness-per-rupee element on the whole site and it needs updating once a year, which is a cadence a non-technical professor will actually sustain.

ALUMNI: build a table, not a photo grid, and make CURRENT PLACEMENT the payoff column. Recommended shape, merging Kording + Saskatchewan + Princeton: `Name | Degree, year | Thesis/project title | Now: role, organisation`. All four fields already exist for the six graduated PhDs and nine graduated MTechs except the last — collect it once via a WhatsApp/email round to former students and it becomes the strongest section on the site. Group by PhD / MTech / Intern; no photos; sort newest first.

Put the alumni section ON the RAFT page as an anchored section rather than on a separate /alumni page. Separate alumni pages get no traffic; an anchor from the people section gets scrolled through by every prospective student, which is exactly the audience the placement data is for.

NEWS: run ONE reverse-chronological feed and put its most recent 5–6 items directly on the homepage (Princeton Visual AI's 'RECENT TIMELINE' model) with a '/news' archive behind it. Format per item: date on the left in a fixed format, a 1–2 line headline, an optional link, an optional small thumbnail. Do not group by year headers — a continuous run (AIT ETH) hides gaps better than year buckets, which advertise a thin year.

Seed the news feed with 15–20 backdated real items before launch (past defences, past paper acceptances, past awards, students joining) so it never launches empty. Then give the professor an explicit list of the eight event types that warrant a post — paper accepted, student joined, student defended, award/fellowship, invited talk or conference, fieldwork/campaign, new grant, media coverage — because the failure mode is not laziness, it's not knowing what counts as news.

Never render a 'last updated' date or a visible year gap on the news feed. If the newest item is more than ~4 months old, the design should degrade gracefully — e.g. the homepage shows the news strip without dates in large type, or falls back to featuring recent publications instead. Sparse feeds look dead mainly because the dates are shouting.

PUBLICATIONS: group by year, reverse-chron; each entry = title, authors with RAFT members' names bolded, venue + year, DOI link, and a row of small resource chips (PDF / Data / Code / Media) where they exist (UW IDL model). Bolding the group's own names in a long author list is the single cheapest way to make a shared publication list legible. Add a 'selected' flag column in the source sheet so ~8 papers can be featured on the homepage while the full list lives on /publications.

PROJECTS & FUNDING: split into 'Ongoing' and 'Completed' (SCI-Hy model). Per project show title, funder name, years, a one-line aim, and the RAFT people on it. Put funder names in the project entries themselves and add a single 'Support' line at the foot of the RAFT page listing sponsors as text, tagged current vs past (Princeton Visual AI model). Skip grant numbers — no lab I fetched displays them.

JOIN / OPPORTUNITIES: keep the existing subject-line convention — the current page asks candidates to email with subject 'Looking for an Opportunity' and to include research interests, background and skills, motivation, and desired learning outcomes and contributions. That is already better than most lab pages. Render the subject line as a copyable code block, and add the Terrer-Lab move: name the SPECIFIC Indian and international routes with their approximate deadlines (IIT Hyderabad PhD admission cycles, PMRF, CSIR/UGC-NET JRF, DST INSPIRE, Newton-Bhabha / Marie Skłodowska-Curie for incoming postdocs) and one line of fit guidance each. Naming real schemes with real deadlines is what separates a joining page from a form letter.

ADD A 'LAB LIFE' STRIP (not a whole page unless there are enough photos) — 4–6 captioned candids of fieldwork, gauge installation, viva celebrations, conference trips — with one line of framing text and a link to Join. Field photography is a genuine advantage in hydrology and it is what will make this site unmistakably real rather than generated.

Add ONE personality token per person — a two-word non-research interest, UW IDL style. It is a trivial extra column in the people sheet and it is the detail most reliably absent from AI-generated and template sites.

GOOGLE SHEETS SCHEMA — design the sheets around these patterns now, so the front end never has to be restructured. People sheet columns: `id, name, tier (PI/PhD/MTech/Intern/Alumni-PhD/Alumni-MTech), status (current/past), start_year, end_year, degree, topic_or_thesis, photo_file, email, scholar_url, website_url, current_role, current_org, current_org_url, interests, order`. News sheet: `date, headline, body, link, type, image_file, featured`. Projects sheet: `title, funder, start_year, end_year, status, one_liner, people_ids, image_file`. Publications sheet: `year, title, authors, venue, doi, pdf_url, data_url, code_url, selected`. The `current_role` / `current_org` pair is the field that makes the alumni section outclass Stanford HCI's, so make it a required column in the sheet's data-validation.

Because raftwaters.in does not currently resolve, treat the RAFT page as self-sufficient: complete on its own, with the outbound link presented as a modest 'RAFT group site →' rather than as a call to action the whole page funnels into. Verify the domain is live before launch.

Allocate visual weight deliberately, DeepMind-style: one flagship item gets a large image (SnapFlood or the flood information system), news and projects get medium thumbnails, publications get text only. Resisting the urge to give every item an identical card is the main thing separating an editorially designed lab page from a template.

## Pattern 1 — Alumni with current placement

The differentiator. Four verified formats, ordered by information density:

**Princeton Visual AI Lab** (`/people.html`) — alumni subdivided by education level (postdocs, PhD, Master's, undergrad, high-school interns). Entries carry degree tier, years, thesis title in italics, and current placement:
- `Dr. Sunnie S. Y. Kim — PH.D. DEGREE 2025 — Advancing Responsible AI with Human-Centered Evaluation — Research Scientist at Apple`
- `Dr. Ye Zhu — POSTDOC 2023-2025 — Monge Tenure-Track Assistant Professor in Computer Science at École Polytechnique in Paris`

Current members by contrast carry only title/position: `Dr. Esin Tureci / Senior Researcher`. Note the inversion — alumni get MORE metadata than current members, because the placement is the argument for joining.

**Kording Lab** (`/people/`) — alumni as a three-column table:
`Tony Liu | Graduate Student (2018-2024) | Assistant Professor of Computer Science, Mount Holyoke College`
Current members get only a photo and a linked name. Same inversion.

**AIT ETH** (`/people`) — 'Previous Members' organised by departure year 2014–2025, with 'Now at' phrasing and a hyperlink to the new employer:
`2020 - 2025 — Dr. Zijian Dong — Now at PicoXR (ByteDance)`
Separate sub-lists for 'Previous Guests' and 'Previous Interns'.

**Centre for Hydrology, U. Saskatchewan** (`/people/alumni.php`) — two tables, no photos at all. Former Post-Doctoral Fellows: `Dr Chris Marsh | Research Scientist, Environment and Climate Change Canada`. Former Post-Graduate Students: `Nik Aksamit | PhD, 2017 | Alpine Boundary Layer Turbulence and Snow Transport | Post-Doc, Centre for Hydrology` and `Warren Helgason | PhD, 2009 | Energy Fluxes at the Air-Snow Interface | Associate Professor, Department of Agricultural and Bioresource Engineering, U of S`. This is the closest structural match to what Satish's existing student data already supports.

**CU Boulder Mountain Hydrology** — alumni in an expandable accordion, prose format: `Patrick Saylor, MA 2024 in Geography. Hydrologist with NRCS Snow Surveys` / `Emily Baker, MA 2015 in Geography; Now at USGS Alaska Science Center` / `Adrian Harpold, Director, Nevada Mountain Ecohydrology Lab, Reno, NV`. The accordion keeps a long list from dominating the page — a good option if the alumni list grows past ~25.

**Bhamla Lab** (`/past-lab-members`) — four tiers (Postdocs, Graduate Students, Staff, Undergraduates), plain text, no photos, placements with years in parentheses: `Dr. Jacob Harrison, Assistant Professor of Biology at Morehouse`, `Dr. Yasemin Ozkan-Aydin, Assistant Professor at the University of Notre Dame`, `Kai Yung, PhD Student at UC Irvine`, `Raghav Acharya, NSF GRFP, PhD@MIT (2022)`, `Gaurav Byagathvalli, CEO and co-founder of Piezo Tx (2022)`.

**Yamazaki Lab** — partial: collaborators/former postdocs get placement (`Menaka Revel — (Oct 2023-) Former PostDoc — Researcher @ University of Waterloo`) but 'Former Students' get only name, degree type and graduation date with no employment info. A common half-measure.

**Counter-examples (what not to do):**
- Stanford HCI Group `/people` — alumni are photo + name, nothing else. `Adrian Graham` with a portrait and no link. Affiliated faculty on the same page get full biographical paragraphs; alumni get zero text.
- UW IDL `/people` — alumni are hyperlinked names only; collaborators likewise. Photos appear only for current members.
- Terrer Lab `/team` — alumni rendered as a run-on name list: `Leila Mirzagholi Na Chen Yanlei Feng Trevor Cambron...`
- WRE Lab `/team` — one alumnus (Alexander Tansey) under an 'Alumni' heading with no details, and a 'Postdoc' section header with nobody under it.
- MIT Media Lab City Science `/people` — past members remain inline in the alphabetical roster tagged `Chance Jiajie Li, Research Affiliate, Past Member`.

---

## Pattern 2 — People page structure and photo treatment

**Bhamla Lab** `/people` — the tiered-density exemplar. Five tiers, four densities:
- Research Scientists & Postdocs (10) and Grad Students (8): individual cards with headshot, name, title, a one-line research description (`Daehyun integrates principles from fluid mechanics and micro-robotics to uncover mechanisms behind animal behavior`), email, Google Scholar and personal site links, and a `Read more →` expander.
- Staff (1): text only.
- Undergraduate Students (46): name + major abbreviation only (`ChBE`, `BME`).
- High School Interns (4): a simple list.

**UW IDL** `/people` — headshot grid of current members at the top, then a detail list of the same people, then alumni as names, then collaborators as names. Detail entries append research interests AND personal interests, comma-separated:
- `Leilani Battle, Professor, UW CSE, Databases, Visualization, HCI, Zombies, Disc Golf`
- `Josh Horowitz, PhD Student, UW CSE, Dynamic Media, End-User Programming, Bikes, Maps`

**AIT ETH** `/people` — circular avatars, left-aligned, single column. Tiers: Faculty (1), Staff (2), Postdocs (1), PhD Students (8), Previous Members (by year), Previous Guests, Previous Interns. Per person: name linked to a profile page, position title, mailto email, and a 'Personal Site' link. Example: `Dr. Juan Zarate — Lab Manager and Scientist — juan.zarate@inf.ethz.ch`.

**CMU HCII** `/people/faculty` and `/people/phd-students` — vertical list, 600x400 landscape headshot crops left of the text, name linked to profile, title, mailto email, and a research-areas filter at the top ('Accessibility and Assistive Technology', 'Data Visualization', 'Human-Centered AI'). Critically, missing photos are filled with `default_images/silhouette2.png` — a grey silhouette. No advisor field.

**Oxford Robotics Institute** `/people/` — A–Z letter index plus role filters (All staff / Academic staff / Research staff / DPhil Candidates / Admin & Support Staff). NO photos. Entries: `Maurice Fallon — Professor of Robotics; PI of Dynamic Robot Systems Group`. Scales to hundreds; reads as a directory.

**WRE Lab** `/team` — headshot above name, and unusually rich per-person prose: pronouns, department, degrees and institutions, previous experience, current interests. Example: Lee Smith is `a third year at Northeastern University majoring in Environmental and Sustainability Science with a concentration in Earth, Oceans, and Environmental Change`. This depth works at 4 people and would be unmaintainable at 20.

**ETH Land-Climate Dynamics** — no per-person cards on the group landing page at all. Two group photographs (August 2024 and 2023) with names listed by row position in the caption, plus a link to a searchable roster.

## Pattern 3 — News / updates feeds

**AIT ETH** `/news` — DD.MM.YY dates (`04.05.26`), thumbnail per item (headshot or conference logo), 1–2 lines, unbroken reverse-chron 2026 → 2013 with no year headers. Verbatim items:
- `Seyedmorteza Sadat passed the doctoral exam. Congratulations!`
- `We have 4 papers accepted at ICCV 2025.`
- `Prof. Dr. Otmar Hilliges is appointed as Full Professor. Congratulations!`
- `Our paper on capturing subjective first-person view videos by drones will be presented at SIGGRAPH'20.`
- `Three new papers accepted at ACM SIGCHI 2015.`

**Princeton Visual AI** homepage — the feed IS the homepage, headed `RECENT TIMELINE`, July 2026 back to August 2025. Each entry: date, linked achievement title, venue + year, author names, image. Items include `July 2026 — Best Paper Award at ICML workshop — Xindi Wu, Olga Russakovsky`, `June 2026 — Outstanding Reviewer Award — Sanghyuk Chun`, `September 2025 — Francis Robbins Upton Fellowship in Engineering — Sanghyuk Chun`. Equal-contribution notation is handled with `* = equal contribution`.

**Terrer Lab** `/news` — date left-aligned, headline, short description, optional `Read more` link. No images inside items. Generous whitespace, clear separation, sparse and scannable. Verbatim: `Farewell to Sara, Diego and Shuai`; `Ruofei Jia has been awarded a Martin Fellowship for the 2026–2027 academic year`; `We have just launched a new Terrer Lab website`; `César Terrer has been named to Clarivate's 2025 Highly Cited Researchers list`.

**UW IDL** — updates use full dates (`October 3, 2025`), reverse-chron, 1–2 lines per entry, covering awards, new publications, achievements.

**Stanford HCI Group** — news as bullets that link career transitions and awards: `Mitchell Gordon joins the faculty at MIT`, `wins Best Paper at UIST 2023`, `named an ACM Fellow`.

**MIT Media Lab City Science** `/updates` — 50+ entries, July 2026 back to September 2024, each with a content-type icon (Video / Article / Post / Gallery), linked title, 1–2 sentence description, date, group tag, and topic tags (`#robotics`, `#design`, `#climate change`) that enable filtered browsing.

**Oxford Robotics Institute** — homepage carousel of 8 news items with thumbnail, date, headline, and category tags (`Public engagement`, `Industry impact`), plus a `View all News` link.

## Pattern 4 — Research themes / thrusts

**Terrer Lab** — three method-based thrusts, each a heading plus one line:
- `Field measurements: Repeated soil and biomass sampling at sites across the world's biomes`
- `Satellites & remote sensing: Global observations of vegetation, carbon, and land-cover change from space`
- `Machine learning & synthesis: Meta-analysis and statistical models that scale field data to the globe`
Hero above them: `How much carbon can land hold, and for how long?` / `We combine field measurements, satellites, and machine learning to quantify the terrestrial carbon sink — and how climate change is reshaping it.` Plus a status banner: `Highly Cited Researcher 2025 — top 1% by citations in field`.

**Ink & Switch** — four pillars each with a custom-drawn SVG mark (not stock icons): Local-first Software, Malleable Software, Programmable Ink, Universal Version Control. Positioning line: `An independent research lab exploring the future of tools for thought.` Featured work as cards tagged by pillar and typed (`Essay`, `Lab Notebook`) with a year. Monochrome palette, generous whitespace, institutional voice — no individual profiles at all, just `hello@inkandswitch.com` plus Bluesky/GitHub.

**Princeton Visual AI** `/research.html` — three thrusts as plain text lines, no imagery whatsoever: `computer vision, machine learning`; `human-computer interaction, cognitive science`; `fairness, accountability, and transparency`.

**MIT Media Lab City Science** — `Group research is organized around six themes:` rendered as cards with title, description, tags, and the names of team members on each.

**WRE Lab** — six project cards in a grid, each with thumbnail, title, 50–80 word description, linked to a detail page. Research nav is a dropdown with named subsections: Mountain Ecohydrology, Wildfire, Hydrologic Ecosystem Services, Other projects.

**CU Boulder Mountain Hydrology** — four thrusts described in prose with a concrete deliverable attached to each, e.g. snow hydrology anchored by `near-real-time snow water equivalent (SWE) estimates at 500-meter resolution`, and named field sites (Storm Peak Lab, Niwot Ridge LTER).

**Campbell-Staton Group** — five themes given evocative editorial titles rather than technical ones: `The biological costs of civil war` (tuskless elephants), `Adapting to life in cities` (urban lizards), `Taking back Chernobyl` (wolves), `Adaptive solutions to pollution` (alligators), `A Land of Open Graves`. Framing line: `Exploring human activity as a force for evolutionary change.` Photography credited by name (Becca Skinner, Day's Edge Productions) — credit lines are themselves an aliveness signal.

**SCI-Hy (Utah State)** `/projects/` — cards with thumbnail + title, split Active / Completed. Funder folded into the title string: `CIROH: Advance water management-hydrologic model coupling to improve hydrologic forecasting in managed watersheds`; `CIROH: Improving low-flow estimates in the NextGen Framework through improved subsurface conceptualization and parameterization`; `Advance the representation of groundwater in a water management system model for the Bear River Watershed`. No grant numbers, no dates, no PI-role field, no sponsor logos on the listing.

**Princeton Visual AI** — a single `ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS` block at the foot of the homepage listing sponsors, split `(current/ongoing)` and `(past)`.

**CU Boulder Mountain Hydrology** — funders named in prose (NSF, NASA, NOAA, USDA) alongside named field sites.

**Yamazaki Lab** — products get their own named blocks rather than being buried in projects: CaMa-Flood (global river model), MERIT DEM/Hydro datasets, SplashTune (an interactive rainfall-runoff game). Community events are listed with a standing cadence: `Hydrosphere Science Seminar ... from 3:00 PM on the first Monday of each month via Zoom`. A recurring public seminar with a fixed slot is another low-cost aliveness device.

**Bhamla Lab** — a `bhamla lab in the media` strip with outlet names (Newsweek, Science Magazine, CNN) tied to specific projects (the $1 hearing aid, cicada jet urination). SVL uses the weaker version: a bare logo wall (CNBC, NYT, Wired, TechCrunch, CBS, Quartz) with no story attached.

## Pattern 6 — Joining / opportunities

**Terrer Lab** `/join` — the gold standard. Year-round openness stated once: `Even if you don't see an open position listed, we are always on the lookout for motivated, talented scientists excited to make an impact in ecology and climate-change research.` Then four named external fellowships:
1. NOAA Climate & Global Change Postdoctoral Fellowship (closes October 16, 2026) — `A strong fit for the lab`
2. MIT Postdoctoral Fellowship Program for Engineering Excellence (deadline ~late January)
3. Marie Skłodowska-Curie Global Fellowships (deadline ~mid-September) — `the natural route for a European researcher to work with us`
4. Schmidt Science Fellows (nomination ~spring) — for those `pivoting into a new field`
Plus: contact the PI early to `shape the proposal and research plan together`. Also a diversity/inclusion/belonging statement.

**WRE Lab** `/open-positions` — most concrete terms. Named PhD position in mountain ecohydrology; `The successful candidate will be supported to design a research project within the broad themes of mountain ecohydrology and water resources that excites them.` Funding: RA/TA support up to five years, competitive stipend, tuition waiver, health insurance, conference funding. Two application routes with two deadlines (MES Dec 1, CEE Dec 15). `While an M.S. is preferred, it is not required.` `Candidates from historically and currently marginalized groups are particularly encouraged to apply.` Separate coastal-hydrology postdoc, `fully funded with a competitive stipend for two years`.

**Bhamla Lab** — invites `curiosity-driven researchers, from undergraduates to postdocs` and asks for CVs, project summaries, and research interest statements; postdoc posting linked as a PDF.

**Stanford NLP** — splits the audience explicitly: `Stanford students: Apply to do research in the Stanford NLP Group` vs external applicants directed to `Apply to Stanford programs in Computer Science or Linguistics`. Splitting internal vs external routes is worth copying — IIT Hyderabad students vs external PhD applicants are different audiences.

**Current Satish site** `/opportunities` — already reasonable: `Our research areas include hydroclimatology, rainfall and flood forecasting and modelling, data science, AI/ML, scientific computing, and the development of useful weather- and hydrology-related products.` / `We aim to translate our research into information and decision-support tools for scientists, engineers, operational agencies, and policymakers.` / invites `sincere, enthusiastic, and self-motivated interns, prospective PhD students, and postdoctoral researchers`. Requires email subject `Looking for an Opportunity` and four content items (research interests, background and skills, motivation, desired learning outcomes and contributions). The subject-line convention is a genuinely good spam filter and should survive the redesign as a copyable block.

**UW IDL** `/papers` — grouped by year, reverse-chron. Per entry: left-aligned thumbnail, linked title (to a paper detail page, not straight to a PDF), author names each individually hyperlinked to their own pages, venue + year, resource links (PDF / Software / Video / Supplementary / Demo / Website), and an award badge where earned. **Stanford HCI Group** — chronological by conference/venue with thumbnails, author names, badges (`best paper`, `Honorable Mention`), and action chips: `TRY IT!` linking to a GitHub repo, `[PROJECT]` linking to a project page.

**AIT ETH** homepage — projects organised by year (2026, 2025, 2024) as thumbnail + title + author names linked to people profiles + venue + resource icons for video, paper, code.

**DeepMind** `/research` — publications reduced to plain text links, deliberately, so that visual weight goes to breakthroughs and news instead.

## Baseline: what already exists on the current Google Site

`/raft` — RAFT = `Rainfall-runoff Analysis modelling and Forecasting Tools (RAFT) Research Team`. Works on `different aspects of rainfall and runoff in both cities and riverine areas` with goals of `collection, analysis, modelling, and development and dissemination of products`. Objective: `develop a flood information system for both cities and riverine areas` enabling dialogue between scientists, engineers, policymakers and citizens. Activities listed: hydrological modelling and forecasting for Indian river basins; urban flood modelling with satellite/remote sensing; hydroclimatological analysis and extreme weather prediction; weather pattern modelling with urban morphology change; ML for runoff estimation; rainfall prediction using radar and deep learning; flood risk mapping for Hyderabad and Kochi. Data collection via the `SnapFlood mobile application`, a Google Form, and social media for uploading `flood relevant media`. Roster: Dr Satish Regonda + 6 PhD scholars (Surya Kiran, Padmini, Saipriya, Lagnajeet, Mohan, Vamshi) + 3 MTech (Swagatam, Kanishka, Shruti).

`/students` — 9 current PhD scholars with research topics (`Saipriya SR, Understanding urban hydroclimatology and modelling of urban floods for the city Hyderabad, India`); current MTech with join year (`Rahul Thangallapally — Joined the M.Tech. program in 2025`); 6 graduated PhD with thesis titles and viva dates (`Vimal Chandra Sharma, Streamflow Forecasting and Flood Inundation Modelling Framework in the Lower Godavari River Basin, India, viva-voice was done in September 2021`); 9 graduated MTech with project titles and graduation years (`B Sreekarthikeya Reddy, Digital Elevation Model from Unmanned Aerial Vehicle: An Application in Urban Flood Modeling, graduated in 2019`); 3 UG mini-project contributors 2019–2020. **No placement data anywhere** — that is the one field to collect.

`/home` nav — Home, Education & Employment, Products & Publications, Research (Urban Flood / SnapFlood / Guidelines for Sixer Twitter), Teaching, Students, RAFT, Opportunities.

Note the mismatch worth resolving: the RAFT page says 6 PhD scholars; the Students page says 9. A single Google Sheet as the source of truth for both the RAFT roster and the Students section fixes this class of drift permanently.

## What makes a lab page feel ALIVE vs a brochure

Concrete, verified signals of aliveness:
1. **Dated events about named people.** `Seyedmorteza Sadat passed the doctoral exam. Congratulations!` (AIT). A brochure says 'our students excel'; an alive page says who defended and when.
2. **Departures and farewells posted as news.** `Farewell to Sara, Diego and Shuai` (Terrer). Brochures never mention people leaving.
3. **Dated candid photos with informal captions.** `Pizza & Science in our new group space` (Terrer, /lab-life). Framing line: `Field trips, dinners, graduations, and the day-to-day of a small international group.`
4. **Dated group photos with row-by-row names**, and last year's kept alongside (ETH Land-Climate Dynamics, August 2024 + 2023).
5. **Non-research personal interests** in people metadata: `Zombies, Disc Golf`, `Bikes, Maps` (UW IDL).
6. **Alumni placements**, which prove the pipeline works and are the thing a prospective PhD student actually wants.
7. **Named specific products with links you can click**: CaMa-Flood, MERIT, SplashTune (Yamazaki); Stanza, DSPy (Stanford NLP); SnapFlood (RAFT).
8. **A standing meeting with a real time slot**: `Fridays 11:30am-12:30pm · Free & open to the public` (Stanford HCI seminar); `first Monday of each month via Zoom` (Yamazaki).
9. **Photography credited to a named person** (Campbell-Staton credits Becca Skinner and Day's Edge Productions).
10. **Specific deadlines and funding numbers** on the join page rather than 'we welcome motivated students'.

Brochure tells:
- Stock icons on research themes.
- A homepage carousel as the primary content (SVL, Yamazaki both do this — it burns the most valuable screen real estate on a slideshow).
- A grey silhouette in place of a missing photo.
- A logo wall of press outlets with no story attached (SVL) instead of media items tied to named projects (Bhamla).
- Alumni as photos with no text, or names with no placement.
- Prose in the passive voice about 'cutting-edge research' with no named person, no date, no number.
- Empty tier headers (a 'Postdoc' heading with nobody under it — WRE Lab).
- A news feed whose most recent item is visibly two years old.

exemplars.name: Princeton Visual AI Lab (Olga Russakovsky), Princeton University
exemplars.what_works: Alumni are subdivided by degree tier (postdoc / PhD / Master's / undergrad / high-school intern) and each entry carries degree, years, thesis title in italics, and current job with employer — e.g. 'Dr. Sunnie S. Y. Kim, PH.D. DEGREE 2025, Advancing Responsible AI with Human-Centered Evaluation, Research Scientist at Apple'. Current members deliberately get LESS metadata (title only). The homepage is a reverse-chronological 'RECENT TIMELINE' rather than a static brochure, and sponsors sit in a footer ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS block tagged '(current/ongoing)' vs '(past)'.
exemplars.steal_this: Invert the usual weighting: give alumni MORE metadata than current members. Degree + year + thesis title + current placement, grouped by degree tier. Satish's existing Students page already has three of those four fields for every graduate.

exemplars.name: Terrer Lab (César Terrer), MIT Civil & Environmental Engineering
exemplars.what_works: The join page names four SPECIFIC external fellowships with real deadlines and a one-line fit note each — NOAA Climate & Global Change Postdoctoral Fellowship (closes October 16, 2026, 'A strong fit for the lab'), MIT Postdoctoral Fellowship for Engineering Excellence (~late January), Marie Skłodowska-Curie Global Fellowships (~mid-September, 'the natural route for a European researcher to work with us'), Schmidt Science Fellows (~spring, for those 'pivoting into a new field') — and tells candidates to make contact early so they can 'shape the proposal and research plan together'.
exemplars.steal_this: Replace 'we welcome motivated students' with a named-scheme table: IIT Hyderabad PhD cycles, PMRF, CSIR/UGC-NET JRF, DST INSPIRE, Newton-Bhabha, MSCA — each with an approximate deadline and one line of fit guidance.

exemplars.name: Terrer Lab (César Terrer), MIT — homepage and Lab Life page
exemplars.what_works: Hero is a question, not a mission statement: 'How much carbon can land hold, and for how long?' followed by the method sentence 'We combine field measurements, satellites, and machine learning to quantify the terrestrial carbon sink — and how climate change is reshaping it.' Three thrusts are method-based prose with one-line descriptions, no icons. A separate Lab Life page carries captioned candids ('Pizza & Science in our new group space') under the framing 'Field trips, dinners, graduations, and the day-to-day of a small international group', ending with 'Want to be part of it? See Join us.'
exemplars.steal_this: Open the RAFT page with a question, then a one-sentence method statement. And build a Lab Life strip of captioned fieldwork candids — the cheapest aliveness lever verified anywhere in this research.

exemplars.name: Kording Lab (Konrad Kording), University of Pennsylvania
exemplars.what_works: Alumni are a three-column table — name (hyperlinked to their site) | role and tenure | current position with linked institution: 'Tony Liu | Graduate Student (2018-2024) | Assistant Professor of Computer Science, Mount Holyoke College'. Current members get only a headshot and a linked name. The table format is scannable, sortable-looking, and adds zero visual weight per row.
exemplars.steal_this: The exact three-column alumni table shape. It maps cleanly onto Google Sheets columns (name, role+years, current_role + current_org) so the professor can maintain it without touching HTML.

exemplars.name: AIT Lab (Otmar Hilliges), ETH Zurich
exemplars.what_works: News uses DD.MM.YY dates ('04.05.26'), one small thumbnail per item (usually the person's own headshot), 1–2 lines of text, and an unbroken reverse-chronological run from 2026 back to 2013 with no year headers — so sparse years never announce themselves. Items are ordinary lab life: 'Seyedmorteza Sadat passed the doctoral exam. Congratulations!', 'We have 4 papers accepted at ICCV 2025.' The /people page pairs this with circular avatars and 'Previous Members' by departure year using 'Now at' phrasing: '2020 - 2025, Dr. Zijian Dong, Now at PicoXR (ByteDance)'.
exemplars.steal_this: Continuous reverse-chron news with no year headers, plus the item's own headshot as its thumbnail — it means every news item is also a face, which makes a thin feed look populated.

exemplars.name: Bhamla Lab (Saad Bhamla), Georgia Tech
exemplars.what_works: Four different information densities on one people page: postdocs and grad students get full cards (headshot, one-line research description, email, Scholar link, 'Read more'); staff get text only; 46 undergraduates get name + major abbreviation ('ChBE', 'BME'); high-school interns get a bare list. Missing photos are simply absent rather than replaced with placeholders. Past members live on a separate text-only page with placements and years: 'Dr. Jacob Harrison, Assistant Professor of Biology at Morehouse', 'Gaurav Byagathvalli, CEO and co-founder of Piezo Tx (2022)'.
exemplars.steal_this: Tiered density — full cards for PhD scholars, compact text lines for MTech and interns. It is the only pattern I found that keeps a people page readable as headcount doubles.

exemplars.name: UW Interactive Data Lab (Jeffrey Heer), University of Washington
exemplars.what_works: Publications grouped by year, reverse-chron; each entry is thumbnail + linked title (to a paper page, not a raw PDF) + individually hyperlinked author names + venue and year + a chip row of PDF / Software / Demo / Video / Website + an award badge where earned. The people page appends non-research personal interests to each member's line — 'Leilani Battle, Professor, UW CSE, Databases, Visualization, HCI, Zombies, Disc Golf'.
exemplars.steal_this: The resource-chip row on every publication (PDF / Data / Code / Media), plus two words of personal interest per person on the people page. Both are tiny and both are things a template can't fake.

exemplars.name: Centre for Hydrology, University of Saskatchewan
exemplars.what_works: Two photo-free alumni tables — Former Post-Doctoral Fellows (name | next position) and Former Post-Graduate Students (name | degree, year | thesis title | current position). Example: 'Warren Helgason | PhD, 2009 | Energy Fluxes at the Air-Snow Interface | Associate Professor, Department of Agricultural and Bioresource Engineering, U of S'. No photos at all, which is exactly right — the information is the point and the page stays fast and dense.
exemplars.steal_this: The four-column hydrology-specific alumni table. This is the closest structural match to the data Satish already publishes for his six graduated PhDs and nine graduated MTech students.

exemplars.name: Ink & Switch (independent research lab)
exemplars.what_works: Four research pillars — Local-first Software, Malleable Software, Programmable Ink, Universal Version Control — each with a bespoke hand-drawn SVG mark rather than a stock icon set. Featured work is cards tagged by pillar and typed ('Essay', 'Lab Notebook') with a year. Monochrome, generous whitespace, institutional voice throughout. Positioning line: 'An independent research lab exploring the future of tools for thought.'
exemplars.steal_this: Commission four custom SVG glyphs for the RAFT thrusts instead of using an icon library. Also: labelling every piece of output by TYPE ('Essay', 'Lab Notebook') is a good model for tagging blog posts vs papers vs data releases.

exemplars.name: Mountain Hydrology Group (Noah Molotch), INSTAAR, CU Boulder
exemplars.what_works: Alumni sit in an expandable accordion with degree, year, field, and current position in one prose line — 'Patrick Saylor, MA 2024 in Geography. Hydrologist with NRCS Snow Surveys', 'Emily Baker, MA 2015 in Geography; Now at USGS Alaska Science Center'. Research thrusts each carry a concrete deliverable (near-real-time SWE at 500 m resolution) and named field sites (Storm Peak Lab, Niwot Ridge LTER); funders named in prose (NSF, NASA, NOAA, USDA).
exemplars.steal_this: The accordion for a long alumni list — it keeps the section on the main page without letting it dominate — and the habit of anchoring each research thrust to one concrete deliverable and one named field site.

exemplars.name: Google DeepMind research
exemplars.what_works: Visual weight is allocated strictly by importance: flagship 'Breakthroughs' get full-width 1440x810 hero images with a title and a descriptive subtitle ('An agent that plays, reasons, and learns with you in virtual 3D worlds'); 'Latest News' gets 704x704 thumbnails in a grid with category tags and month-year dates; publications are plain text links with no imagery at all.
exemplars.steal_this: Progressive visual richness. One flagship item (SnapFlood / the flood information system) gets the big image; news and projects get medium thumbnails; publications get text. Refusing to give every item an identical card is the main thing separating an edited page from a template.

exemplars.name: Land-Climate Dynamics Group (Sonia Seneviratne), ETH Zurich
exemplars.what_works: The group landing page carries no individual cards at all — instead, two dated group photographs (August 2024 and 2023) with names listed by row position in the caption, plus a link to a searchable roster. Nearly zero maintenance, every face present, and keeping the previous year's photo alongside signals continuity.
exemplars.steal_this: A dated group photo with row-by-row name captions, with last year's kept below it. For a 12-person Indian research group where individual headshot quality will vary wildly, this may be a better primary image than 12 separate portraits.

pitfalls: Grey silhouette placeholders for missing headshots — CMU HCII serves `default_images/silhouette2.png` and it makes the directory look half-built. Every well-handled site simply omits the photo instead. If a visual is needed, use a typographic initials tile.

Alumni as photo + name with no placement (Stanford HCI Group's /people does exactly this: 'Adrian Graham', a portrait, nothing else). Maximum visual weight for zero information — and it wastes the one section prospective students care most about.
Alumni as an undifferentiated comma-blob — Terrer Lab's team page renders them as 'Leila Mirzagholi Na Chen Yanlei Feng Trevor Cambron...'. Unparseable, and it reads as an afterthought.
Stub sections and empty tier headers — WRE Lab has an 'Alumni' heading with one bare name and a 'Postdoc' heading with nobody under it. An empty tier is worse than no tier; it advertises a gap.

A homepage carousel as the primary content (Stanford Vision Lab and Yamazaki Lab both do this). It burns the most valuable screen real estate on a slideshow, and it is one of the strongest 'this is a template' tells.
Alphabetical A–Z directory treatment for a small group — Oxford Robotics Institute's letter index and role filters work at 100+ people and would make a 12-person team read as cold and institutional.

A press-logo wall with no story attached (Stanford Vision Lab shows CNBC / NYT / Wired / TechCrunch / CBS / Quartz logos as bare links). Bhamla Lab's version — outlet name tied to the specific project it covered — is strictly better.
Stock icon sets on research thrusts. Every strong example either uses real field/model imagery, custom-drawn marks, or nothing at all.

A news feed whose most recent item is visibly stale. Year headers make this worse by advertising thin years; a continuous reverse-chron run (AIT ETH) hides gaps better. Never render a 'last updated' stamp.
Generic academic Jekyll/Hugo templates (the al-folio and Hugo Academic look) — instantly recognisable to anyone in the field. The USU SCI-Hy site is competent but reads as template-derived on sight.

Grant numbers, PI-role designations, and sponsor logo walls. No lab I fetched displays grant numbers on the website; they belong on the CV. Funder NAMES in project entries plus one text-only 'Support' line is the pattern that works.

Building the RAFT page as a second faculty bio. Nothing on it should repeat Satish's education, employment history, or personal publication list — those live on his own pages and the duplication is what makes group pages feel like padding.
Splitting alumni onto a separate page nobody visits. Keep them as an anchored section on the RAFT page, in the scroll path of every prospective student.

Duplicating each publication as both a card and a text entry (UW IDL does this for accessibility). It is defensible but it doubles page length and can read as clutter if the two renderings aren't clearly differentiated.

Data drift between pages — the current Google Site's RAFT page says 6 PhD scholars while the Students page says 9. Any design with two hand-maintained rosters will drift again; a single Google Sheet must be the source of truth for both.

Linking prominently to raftwaters.in before it exists. As of 2026-09-04 the domain does not resolve (DNS ENOTFOUND). A dead outbound link on the flagship group page on launch day would be the worst possible first impression.

Asking the professor to maintain long per-person biographies (the WRE Lab model — pronouns, degrees, prior experience, current interests, several sentences each). It is lovely at four people and unmaintainable at twenty. Cap it at one line per person in the sheet.

Over-designing the news item schema. Anything beyond date / headline / optional link / optional image / type tag will not get filled in consistently by a non-technical editor, and half-filled fields look worse than absent ones.
